hypothesis: If the claim holds, the measured surface of an isolated biconcave red cell has mean curvature that varies significantly from point to point, so it is not a constant-mean-curvature surface, and the cell changes to a sphere in hypotonic (diluted) medium.
pass_criterion: In per-cell 3D surface reconstructions of isotonic discocytes, the coefficient of variation of mean curvature H over the membrane surface is at least 0.5 in at least 90% of cells (after excluding rim-edge mesh artefacts). Equivalently, the local H range is at least 3 times the reconstruction noise. In addition, cells in hypotonic medium have sphericity (36*pi*V^2/A^3) of at least 0.9 in at least 80% of cases.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if the median coefficient of variation of H over the surface of isotonic biconcave cells is below 0.1, which means a constant-mean-curvature surface within measurement noise. It is also refuted if fewer than 50% of hypotonic cells reach sphericity of at least 0.9.
interpretation: Thompson's 'surface of equilibrium' for a fluid drop under surface tension alone means a surface of constant mean curvature (Laplace/Young law, with the pressure difference across the interface constant). It maps onto the per-point mean curvature H=(k1+k2)/2 computed from a measured 3D surface mesh or height map of single red cells. 'Diluted blood' maps onto hypotonic medium, where the cell swells and becomes spherical. His proposed alternative forces, osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces, are not tested here. Modern reinterpretation: the red cell membrane is a lipid bilayer with a spectrin cytoskeleton. Its shape is set by bending energy, area-difference elasticity and shear elasticity (Helfrich/Evans-Fung), not by surface tension alone. The geometric part of the claim can also be settled analytically from the Evans-Fung biconcave profile, which gives H varying in sign and magnitude across the cell. That is a calculation, not an empirical dataset test.
no_dataset_reason: I could not verify any public dataset of per-cell 3D red-blood-cell surface reconstructions that covers both isotonic and hypotonic conditions, with a title, landing URL and DOI I am sure resolve. A web search found only candidates I could not confirm. These were a Zenodo record of 3D shape reconstruction from 2D microscopy images, a human RBC hologram dataset, and the data behind a holographic single-shot reconstruction paper (MorpHoloNet). None was verified to hold red-cell surface meshes or height maps with hypotonic labels. Most published quantitative-phase and tomography red-cell data are in paper supplements or are not deposited. Under the rule against fabricating identifiers, I am returning null rather than naming an unverified one.
